title: Signals and Systems 1

sources.title: UCL module catalogue 2026/27: ELEC0006 Signals and Systems 1
sources.used_for: module description and learning outcomes (topic areas), credits, term and assessment

about: ELEC0006 is a half-size (7.5-credit) first-year UCL module taught in Term 2. Its 2026/27 catalogue description covers modelling communication signals in the time and frequency domains and translating between them, how systems manipulate signals, information theory basics, producing, modulating, coding, demodulating and decoding signals in analogue and digital systems, performance limits, design of circuits such as a QAM modulator and single-sideband mixer, and the effect of noise (signal-to-noise ratio and bit error rate). It is taught in person and assessed 60% by exam and 40% by coursework (three assessments) per the 2026/27 catalogue. No ordered syllabus is published, so the topic order here is built from that description.
topics: Fourier series: periodic signals in the frequency domain
The Fourier transform: moving between time and frequency
How systems manipulate signals: LTI systems, convolution and filtering
Analogue modulation and demodulation: AM, DSB-SC, SSB and FM
Digital communications: sampling, coding and digital modulation (including QAM)
Noise, signal-to-noise ratio, link budgets and bit error rate

notes.body:
A communication system moves information from a source to a destination through a channel that adds distortion and noise. The first step is to describe signals mathematically so we can predict what happens to them.

Classifying signals
- Continuous-time (analogue) x(t) versus discrete-time x[n] (samples); digital signals are discrete in time and take values from a finite set.
- Deterministic (fully described by a formula) versus random (described statistically). Information-bearing signals and noise are random; test signals such as sinusoids and pulses are deterministic.
- Periodic, x(t + T) = x(t) for all t, with period T and fundamental frequency f₀ = 1/T; otherwise aperiodic.
- Energy signals have finite total energy E = ∫|x(t)|² dt (e.g. a single pulse). Power signals have finite, non-zero average power P = lim (1/T)∫|x(t)|² dt over a long interval T (e.g. a sinusoid or a long data stream).

The sinusoid: the basic building block
- x(t) = A cos(2πft + φ): amplitude A, frequency f (Hz), angular frequency ω = 2πf (rad/s), phase φ.
- Average power of A cos(2πft + φ) across a 1 Ω reference resistor is A²/2; its rms value is A/√2.
- Complex exponential form: A cos(2πft + φ) = (A/2)e^(j(2πft + φ)) + (A/2)e^(−j(2πft + φ)). A real sinusoid therefore has components at +f and −f; this two-sided view is used throughout spectral analysis.
- Modulation varies A, f or φ of a carrier sinusoid in step with the message.

Decibels
- Power ratio in dB: 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁). Voltage (or amplitude) ratio in dB, across the same impedance: 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁).
- Doubling power is +3.01 dB; doubling voltage is +6.02 dB; ×10 power is +10 dB; ×1000 is +30 dB.
- Absolute power: dBW (relative to 1 W) and dBm (relative to 1 mW). 1 W = 0 dBW = 30 dBm; 1 μW = −30 dBm.
- Gains and losses in dB simply add, which makes chains of amplifiers, cables and propagation paths easy to analyse.

Bandwidth
- The bandwidth of a signal is the range of frequencies containing most of its power. Speech in telephony is limited to about 300–3400 Hz; a baseband signal occupying 0 to W Hz has bandwidth W.
- Channels also have a bandwidth, the range of frequencies they pass. Fitting signals into channel bandwidth, and sharing spectrum between users, is a central theme of the module.

Baseband and passband
- Baseband: signal occupies frequencies near zero (e.g. audio from a microphone).
- Passband: signal is shifted to lie around a carrier frequency f_c (e.g. a radio channel). Modulation moves baseband to passband; demodulation moves it back.

Exam tips: always say whether a dB figure is a power or amplitude ratio; quote power as A²/2 for a sinusoid of amplitude A (normalised to 1 Ω); be ready to sketch a two-sided spectrum.

notes.h: Fourier series: periodic signals as sums of harmonics
notes.body:
Any periodic signal of practical interest can be written as a sum of sinusoids at multiples (harmonics) of its fundamental frequency. This is the first bridge from the time domain to the frequency domain.

Conventions used here
For a signal of period T and fundamental frequency f₀ = 1/T:
- Trigonometric form: x(t) = a₀ + Σ [a_n cos(2πnf₀t) + b_n sin(2πnf₀t)], n = 1, 2, 3, …
  a₀ = (1/T)∫ x(t) dt (the average value), a_n = (2/T)∫ x(t) cos(2πnf₀t) dt, b_n = (2/T)∫ x(t) sin(2πnf₀t) dt, each integral taken over one period.
- Complex exponential form: x(t) = Σ c_n e^(j2πnf₀t), n from −∞ to ∞, with c_n = (1/T)∫ x(t) e^(−j2πnf₀t) dt.
- Link: c₀ = a₀ and, for n ≥ 1, c_n = (a_n − jb_n)/2, c₋ₙ = c_n* for a real signal.
Texts differ (some put a₀/2 as the constant term), so state your convention.

Symmetry shortcuts
- Even signal, x(−t) = x(t): only cosine terms (b_n = 0).
- Odd signal, x(−t) = −x(t): only sine terms (a_n = 0, a₀ = 0).
- Half-wave symmetry, x(t + T/2) = −x(t): only odd harmonics.

Worked example: square wave
A square wave of amplitude ±A, equal to +A for 0 < t < T/2 and −A for T/2 < t < T, is odd with half-wave symmetry. Its series is
- x(t) = (4A/π)[sin(2πf₀t) + (1/3) sin(6πf₀t) + (1/5) sin(10πf₀t) + …]
- so b_n = 4A/(nπ) for odd n and zero for even n. For A = 1 the fundamental amplitude is 4/π ≈ 1.27 (larger than the square wave itself) and the third harmonic is about 0.42.
- The harmonics fall as 1/n because of the sharp jumps; smoother signals (e.g. a triangle wave) have harmonics falling as 1/n², so they need less bandwidth.
- Near a discontinuity a truncated series overshoots by about 9 % of the jump, however many terms are used (the Gibbs phenomenon).

Spectra
- Plotting |c_n| (and the phase ∠c_n) against frequency nf₀ gives a line spectrum: periodic signals contain only discrete frequencies.
- The spacing between lines is f₀ = 1/T: a longer period means more closely spaced lines.

Parseval's theorem for power
- Average power P = (1/T)∫|x(t)|² dt = Σ |c_n|² = a₀² + Σ (a_n² + b_n²)/2.
- For the ±1 square wave, P = 1. The fundamental alone carries (4/π)²/2 ≈ 0.81 of the power; the first three non-zero harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th) carry about 93 %.
- This tells a designer how much bandwidth is needed to pass a signal with acceptable distortion: passing up to the fifth harmonic keeps over 90 % of a square wave's power.

Exam tips: check symmetry first to know which coefficients vanish; integrate over exactly one period; use Parseval to sanity-check coefficients and to answer bandwidth questions.

notes.h: The Fourier transform: moving between time and frequency
notes.body:
Non-periodic signals, such as a single pulse or a stretch of speech, have continuous spectra. The Fourier transform generalises the Fourier series to them.

Convention used here (frequency f in hertz)
- Forward transform: X(f) = ∫ x(t) e^(−j2πft) dt, integral over all t.
- Inverse transform: x(t) = ∫ X(f) e^(j2πft) df, integral over all f.
Some courses use ω instead of f, which introduces a factor 1/(2π) in the inverse transform; results must be adapted if the convention changes.

Key transform pairs (with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx))
- Rectangular pulse of height 1 and width τ, centred at t = 0 ↔ τ sinc(fτ).
- Unit impulse δ(t) ↔ 1 (all frequencies equally).
- Constant 1 ↔ δ(f).
- cos(2πf₀t) ↔ ½[δ(f − f₀) + δ(f + f₀)].
- e^(−at)u(t), a > 0 ↔ 1/(a + j2πf).

Properties (x(t) ↔ X(f))
- Linearity: ax(t) + by(t) ↔ aX(f) + bY(f).
- Time shift: x(t − t₀) ↔ X(f)e^(−j2πft₀): delay changes phase only, not magnitude.
- Frequency shift (modulation): x(t)e^(j2πf_ct) ↔ X(f − f_c), and x(t)cos(2πf_ct) ↔ ½[X(f − f_c) + X(f + f_c)]. This is the mathematical basis of AM and mixers.
- Time scaling: x(at) ↔ (1/|a|)X(f/a): compressing a signal in time spreads its spectrum.
- Duality: if x(t) ↔ X(f) then X(t) ↔ x(−f). A sinc pulse in time has a rectangular spectrum.
- Convolution: x(t) * y(t) ↔ X(f)Y(f); multiplication: x(t)y(t) ↔ X(f) * Y(f).
- Real signals: X(−f) = X*(f), so the magnitude spectrum is even and the phase is odd.
- Rayleigh (Parseval) energy theorem: ∫|x(t)|² dt = ∫|X(f)|² df.

The time–bandwidth trade-off
- A rectangular pulse of width τ has its first spectral nulls at f = ±1/τ; the main lobe (null to null) is 2/τ wide and contains about 90 % of the pulse energy.
- Example: a 1 ms pulse has first nulls at ±1 kHz. Halving the pulse width doubles the bandwidth.
- Consequence: sending data faster (shorter pulses) needs more bandwidth. This links directly to data-rate limits later.

Periodic signals and the transform
A periodic signal's transform is a train of impulses at the harmonic frequencies, weighted by the Fourier series coefficients: X(f) = Σ c_n δ(f − nf₀). So the series is a special case of the transform.

Using the properties: example
Find the spectrum of a 1 ms rectangular pulse multiplied by cos(2π × 100 kHz × t). The pulse alone gives 10⁻³ sinc(10⁻³f). Multiplying by the cosine shifts half of this to +100 kHz and half to −100 kHz: X(f) = 0.5 × 10⁻³[sinc(10⁻³(f − 10⁵)) + sinc(10⁻³(f + 10⁵))]. The radio pulse occupies about 99–101 kHz (main lobe).

Exam tips: quote the convention you use; when finding a transform, try to build the signal from known pairs and properties instead of integrating from scratch; check the units (X(f) of a voltage signal is in V/Hz, i.e. V s).

notes.h: How systems manipulate signals: LTI systems, convolution and filtering
notes.body:
Communication systems are chains of blocks (amplifiers, filters, channels, mixers) that act on signals. The most useful model of a block is the linear time-invariant (LTI) system.

LTI properties
- Linearity: if x₁ → y₁ and x₂ → y₂, then ax₁ + bx₂ → ay₁ + by₂ (superposition).
- Time invariance: if x(t) → y(t), then x(t − t₀) → y(t − t₀).
- Causality: the output never depends on future inputs; for an LTI system this means h(t) = 0 for t < 0.
- BIBO stability: every bounded input gives a bounded output; for an LTI system this requires ∫|h(t)| dt < ∞.

Impulse response and convolution
- The impulse response h(t) is the output when the input is δ(t). For an LTI system it describes the system completely.
- For any input, the output is the convolution y(t) = (x * h)(t) = ∫ x(τ)h(t − τ) dτ.
- Graphical method: flip h, slide it by t, multiply by x and integrate the overlap.
- Discrete-time version: y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k]. Example: x = [1, 2, 1] and h = [1, 1] give y = [1, 3, 3, 1]. The output length is the sum of the lengths minus one.

Frequency response
- Taking Fourier transforms, Y(f) = H(f)X(f), where H(f) is the transform of h(t). Convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency.
- Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions: e^(j2πft) → H(f)e^(j2πft). So for a real system an input A cos(2πft + φ) gives A|H(f)| cos(2πft + φ + ∠H(f)): same frequency, scaled amplitude, shifted phase. An LTI system can never create new frequencies.
- Laplace convention used here: the one-sided transform H(s) = ∫ h(t)e^(−st) dt from t = 0 to ∞, with zero initial conditions. For a causal, stable LTI system (all poles in the left half-plane) the frequency response equals H(s) evaluated at s = j2πf (or s = jω).

Example: first-order RC low-pass filter
- h(t) = (1/RC)e^(−t/RC)u(t) and H(f) = 1/(1 + j2πfRC). The cut-off is f_c = 1/(2πRC), where |H| = 1/√2 (−3 dB).
- A sinusoid at f = 2f_c emerges with |H| = 1/√5 ≈ 0.447 and phase −63.4°.

Filters in communications
- Ideal low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop filters pass or block bands sharply; real filters have a transition band.
- Uses: limiting noise bandwidth at a receiver, removing unwanted mixer products, separating channels, anti-aliasing before sampling, and shaping pulses to control bandwidth.

Distortionless transmission
- A system passes a signal without distortion if, across the signal's band, H(f) = K e^(−j2πft_d): constant gain K and phase linear in frequency (a pure delay t_d). The output is then K x(t − t_d).
- Gain varying with frequency gives amplitude distortion; non-linear phase gives phase (delay) distortion, which smears pulses and causes intersymbol interference in data links.

Non-linear and time-varying systems
- Squaring or multiplying signals creates new frequencies. A mixer multiplies the signal by a local oscillator: cos A cos B = ½[cos(A − B) + cos(A + B)], producing sum and difference frequencies. Modulators and demodulators rely on this, so they are deliberately not LTI.
- Amplifier non-linearity creates harmonics and intermodulation products, which can interfere with neighbouring channels.

Exam tips: state "for an LTI system" before using convolution or H(f); for sinusoidal inputs use |H| and ∠H directly; remember that only non-linear or time-varying blocks create new frequencies.

Information theory, founded by Claude Shannon in 1948, measures information and sets the ultimate limits on how much data a channel can carry.

Information and entropy
- The self-information of an event of probability p is I = log₂(1/p) bits. Rare events carry more information; a certain event carries none.
- A source emitting symbols with probabilities p₁, p₂, …, p_M has entropy H = −Σ p_i log₂ p_i bits per symbol, the average information per symbol.
- H is maximised, at log₂ M, when all M symbols are equally likely. A fair coin gives 1 bit; a biased coin with p = 0.1 gives only about 0.47 bits per toss.
- Example: probabilities ½, ¼, ⅛, ⅛ give H = 0.5 × 1 + 0.25 × 2 + 0.125 × 3 + 0.125 × 3 = 1.75 bits/symbol, against 2 bits for a fixed-length code for four symbols.

Source coding (compression)
- Shannon's source coding theorem: a source cannot be losslessly encoded with fewer than H bits per symbol on average, and codes can approach H.
- Variable-length codes give short codewords to likely symbols. A Huffman code for the example above is 0, 10, 110, 111, with average length 0.5 × 1 + 0.25 × 2 + 0.25 × 3 = 1.75 bits, exactly the entropy (because all probabilities are powers of ½).
- Prefix-free codes (no codeword is the start of another) can be decoded without separators.

Channel coding (error control)
- Redundancy is deliberately added so errors can be detected or corrected: a parity bit detects any single error; repetition and Hamming codes correct errors at the cost of a lower code rate (information bits divided by transmitted bits).

Channel capacity
- The Shannon–Hartley theorem gives the capacity of a channel of bandwidth B (Hz) with additive white Gaussian noise and signal-to-noise power ratio S/N:
  C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bits per second.
- Shannon showed that error-free transmission (with suitable coding) is possible at any rate below C and impossible above it.
- Example: a telephone channel with B = 3.1 kHz and S/N = 30 dB (1000) gives C = 3100 × log₂(1001) ≈ 30.9 kb/s.
- Use the linear ratio, not dB, inside the logarithm. At high SNR each extra 3 dB adds about B bits/s; doubling bandwidth (at the same S/N) doubles capacity, but in practice more bandwidth admits more noise, so S/N falls.

Nyquist signalling rate
- An ideal baseband channel of bandwidth B can carry at most 2B independent symbols per second without intersymbol interference (the Nyquist rate).
- With M signal levels, each symbol carries log₂ M bits, so bit rate ≤ 2B log₂ M. Example: B = 4 kHz with 4 levels gives at most 16 kb/s. Raising M raises the rate only if the SNR is high enough to distinguish the levels, which is where Shannon's limit takes over.

Exam tips: use log₂ (log₂ x = log₁₀ x / log₁₀ 2); convert dB to a ratio before using Shannon–Hartley; remember that capacity is a limit for the AWGN channel, not the rate of any particular modulation scheme.

notes.h: Analogue modulation and demodulation: AM, DSB-SC, SSB and FM
notes.body:
Modulation shifts a baseband message m(t), of bandwidth W, onto a carrier at frequency f_c so it can be radiated efficiently and share the spectrum with other users. Demodulation recovers m(t).

Conventional AM (double sideband with carrier)
- s(t) = A_c[1 + k_a m(t)] cos(2πf_ct). For a single tone, s(t) = A_c[1 + μ cos(2πf_mt)] cos(2πf_ct), where μ is the modulation index (modulation depth).
- Expanding with the product-to-sum identity: a carrier at f_c (amplitude A_c) and two sidebands at f_c ± f_m, each of amplitude μA_c/2.
- Bandwidth: 2W (twice the highest message frequency).
- Measuring μ from the envelope: μ = (A_max − A_min)/(A_max + A_min). An envelope swinging between 15 V and 5 V gives μ = 10/20 = 0.5.
- Power (tone): total = P_c(1 + μ²/2), where P_c is the carrier power. Power efficiency (sideband power/total) = μ²/(2 + μ²): 33.3 % at μ = 1 and only 11.1 % at μ = 0.5. Most of the power sits in the carrier, which carries no information.
- If μ > 1 (overmodulation), the envelope no longer follows the message and an envelope detector distorts.
- Envelope detector: a diode, then an RC network with 1/f_c ≪ RC ≪ 1/W, follows the peaks. It is very cheap, which is why AM broadcasting used it, but it requires μ ≤ 1.

DSB-SC (double sideband, suppressed carrier)
- s(t) = A_c m(t) cos(2πf_ct), produced by a multiplier (balanced modulator). Same 2W bandwidth, but no wasted carrier power.
- Needs coherent (synchronous) detection: multiply by a local carrier cos(2πf_ct + φ) and low-pass filter. The product is ½A_c m(t)[cos φ + cos(4πf_ct + φ)]; the filter leaves ½A_c m(t) cos φ. A phase error φ reduces the output, and φ = 90° gives zero, so the receiver must lock its oscillator to the carrier.

SSB (single sideband)
- Sends only one sideband: bandwidth W, half that of AM or DSB-SC, and lower noise bandwidth.
- Filter method: generate DSB-SC and remove one sideband with a sharp band-pass filter (easiest when the message has no very low-frequency content, e.g. speech above 300 Hz).
- Phasing (Hartley) method: s(t) = m(t) cos(2πf_ct) ∓ m̂(t) sin(2πf_ct), where m̂ is m with every component shifted by −90° (Hilbert transform). The minus sign gives the upper sideband, the plus sign the lower.
- Tone check: cos(2πf_mt)cos(2πf_ct) − sin(2πf_mt)sin(2πf_ct) = cos(2π(f_c + f_m)t), a single line at f_c + f_m.
- Demodulation is coherent, as for DSB-SC.

Mixers and the superheterodyne receiver
- A mixer multiplies the incoming signal by a local oscillator (LO) and produces sum and difference frequencies. Choosing f_LO lets a receiver shift any channel to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF) where filtering and amplification are easier.
- Example: with f_RF = 100 MHz and f_LO = 110.7 MHz, the IF is 10.7 MHz. A signal at 121.4 MHz (the image frequency, f_LO + IF) would also produce 10.7 MHz, so it must be removed by filtering before the mixer.

Frequency modulation (FM)
- The instantaneous frequency is f_c + k_f m(t). For a tone, the peak frequency deviation is Δf and the modulation index is β = Δf/f_m.
- Carson's rule estimates the bandwidth: B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m). Broadcast FM with Δf = 75 kHz and f_m = 15 kHz needs about 180 kHz.
- FM has a constant envelope (so it tolerates amplifier non-linearity) and trades extra bandwidth for better noise performance.

Exam tips: show the product-to-sum step when finding spectra; give bandwidths (AM 2W, DSB-SC 2W, SSB W, FM by Carson); remember the efficiency formula applies to tone modulation.

notes.h: Digital communications: sampling, coding and digital modulation
notes.body:
Most modern systems convert analogue messages into bits, then transmit the bits by digital modulation. This topic follows that chain and ends with the design of a QAM modulator.

Sampling
- Sampling theorem: a signal band-limited to W Hz can be reconstructed exactly from samples taken at f_s > 2W (the Nyquist rate is 2W).
- Sampling makes copies of the spectrum at multiples of f_s. If f_s < 2W the copies overlap: aliasing. A component at f appears at |f − kf_s| for the integer k that puts it in 0 to f_s/2. Example: a 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz appears at 3 kHz.
- An analogue anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the sampler removes components above f_s/2.

Quantisation and PCM
- Each sample is rounded to one of L = 2ⁿ levels and coded as n bits: pulse-code modulation (PCM).
- Bit rate = n f_s. Telephone speech: 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kb/s. CD audio: 44.1 kHz × 16 bits × 2 channels ≈ 1.41 Mb/s.
- Quantisation error behaves like noise. For a full-scale sinusoid and a uniform quantiser, SQNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB: about 50 dB for 8 bits and 98 dB for 16 bits. Each extra bit adds about 6 dB.

Line coding
Bits are sent at baseband as pulses: NRZ (non-return-to-zero), Manchester (a transition in every bit, easing clock recovery and removing DC) and others. The choice affects bandwidth, DC content and timing recovery.

Digital modulation
- ASK (amplitude-shift keying; on–off keying is the simplest form), FSK (frequency-shift keying) and PSK (phase-shift keying). BPSK uses two phases, 0° and 180°; QPSK uses four, carrying 2 bits per symbol.
- M-ary schemes send k = log₂ M bits per symbol, so bit rate R_b = R_s log₂ M, where R_s is the symbol (baud) rate.
- A constellation diagram plots each symbol as a point (I, Q) in the plane of the in-phase (cosine) and quadrature (sine) components. Gray coding labels neighbouring points with bit patterns differing in one bit, so the most likely symbol error causes only one bit error.
- QAM (quadrature amplitude modulation) varies both amplitude and phase. 16-QAM is a 4 × 4 grid carrying 4 bits per symbol; 64-QAM carries 6. Denser constellations carry more bits per hertz but points are closer together, so they need a higher SNR for the same error rate.

Bandwidth of digital signals
- With raised-cosine pulse shaping of roll-off α (0 ≤ α ≤ 1), the passband bandwidth is B = R_s(1 + α).
- Example: 16-QAM at 1 Mbaud carries 4 Mb/s; with α = 0.25 it occupies 1.25 MHz, a spectral efficiency of 3.2 b/s/Hz.

Designing a QAM modulator
- Serial-to-parallel converter splits the bit stream; for 16-QAM, 2 bits go to the I branch and 2 to the Q branch.
- Each pair is mapped (Gray coded) to one of four levels, e.g. −3, −1, +1, +3.
- Pulse-shaping (raised-cosine) filters limit bandwidth.
- The I signal multiplies cos(2πf_ct) and the Q signal multiplies the carrier shifted by 90°; with the convention s(t) = I(t)cos(2πf_ct) − Q(t)sin(2πf_ct), the two are subtracted.
- Demodulation: multiply s(t) by 2cos(2πf_ct) and low-pass filter to obtain I(t); multiply by −2sin(2πf_ct) and low-pass filter to obtain Q(t). These work because the products contain I or Q at baseband plus terms at 2f_c, which the filter removes. Then sample at the symbol centres and choose the nearest constellation point.
- The local carrier must be phase-locked to the transmitter's (carrier recovery), and symbol timing recovered; otherwise the constellation rotates or smears.

Exam tips: always check f_s > 2W; give bit rate = R_s log₂ M; draw the I/Q block diagram with the 90° shifter and low-pass filters clearly labelled.

notes.h: Noise, signal-to-noise ratio, link budgets and bit error rate
notes.body:
Every receiver adds noise, and noise sets the ultimate performance of a communication link: how far it can reach, how fast it can go and how many errors it makes.

Thermal noise
- Random electron motion in any resistor at absolute temperature T produces noise with a flat (white) spectrum. Available noise power in bandwidth B: N = kTB, with Boltzmann's constant k ≈ 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
- At T = 290 K, kT ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz, i.e. about −174 dBm/Hz. In 1 MHz the noise is about −114 dBm.
- Noise power is proportional to bandwidth, so receivers filter to the signal bandwidth and no wider.
- Additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) is the standard channel model.

Signal-to-noise ratio
- SNR = S/N (signal power over noise power), usually in dB: 10 log₁₀(S/N).
- Noise figure F (dB) of an amplifier: how much it degrades SNR, F = SNR_in/SNR_out (linear), referred to a 290 K source. For a cascade, F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + … (Friis noise formula), so the first stage's noise figure and gain matter most; this is why a low-noise amplifier sits directly after the antenna.
- Equivalent noise temperature is used in satellite work: N = kT_sysB.

Link budgets (free-space links)
- Received power in dB: P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r − L_fs − L_other, with gains in dBi and powers in dBW or dBm.
- Free-space path loss (far field, between isotropic antennas): L_fs = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) dB. It grows by 6 dB each time distance or frequency doubles.
- Worked satellite example (illustrative values): geostationary distance d ≈ 36 000 km, f = 12 GHz (λ = 2.5 cm) gives L_fs ≈ 205.2 dB. With P_t = 100 W (20 dBW), G_t = 30 dBi and G_r = 40 dBi, P_r ≈ 20 + 30 + 40 − 205.2 ≈ −115.2 dBW. With system noise temperature 150 K and B = 36 MHz, N = kTB ≈ 7.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ W ≈ −131.3 dBW, so SNR ≈ 16.1 dB.
- System limits follow from the budget: more distance, higher frequency (for fixed antenna gains) or wider bandwidth all reduce SNR; bigger dishes, more power or lower-noise receivers increase it.

Bit error rate
- In a digital link noise occasionally pushes a received sample across a decision boundary, causing a bit error. BER is the long-run fraction of bits in error.
- The relevant measure is E_b/N₀: energy per bit over the noise power spectral density. It relates to SNR by E_b/N₀ = SNR × (B/R_b).
- For BPSK with coherent detection in AWGN, P_b = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)), where Q(x) is the tail probability of a standard Gaussian. Gray-coded QPSK has the same BER per bit as BPSK at the same E_b/N₀.
- Reference points (BPSK, AWGN): E_b/N₀ ≈ 9.6 dB gives P_b ≈ 10⁻⁵; about 10.5 dB gives 10⁻⁶. Every extra dB near this region reduces BER substantially (the curve is steep).
- Higher-order schemes (16-QAM, 64-QAM) need more E_b/N₀ for the same BER because constellation points are closer together; FSK and non-coherent detection also need more.
- Error-correcting codes reduce the E_b/N₀ needed for a target BER (coding gain), at the cost of extra redundant bits.

Analogue performance
For analogue systems the output SNR is the figure of merit; AM with envelope detection is relatively noisy because power is wasted in the carrier, while wideband FM improves output SNR at the cost of bandwidth.

Exam tips: keep units consistent (dBW vs dBm differ by 30 dB); add gains and subtract losses in dB; state "coherent BPSK in AWGN" when quoting the Q-function BER formula.

cards.f: Power of A cos(2πft + φ) (1 Ω reference)
cards.b: A²/2; the rms value is A/√2.

cards.f: dB for power and amplitude ratios
cards.b: Power: 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁). Amplitude (same impedance): 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁).
Power relative to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W, −30 dBm = 1 μW.
Energy signal: finite total energy (e.g. a pulse). Power signal: finite non-zero average power (e.g. a sinusoid).
A cos(2πft) = (A/2)e^(j2πft) + (A/2)e^(−j2πft): components of A/2 at ±f.
Baseband occupies frequencies near 0 Hz; passband is centred on a carrier f_c. Modulation shifts baseband to passband.
c_n = (1/T)∫ over one period of x(t)e^(−j2πnf₀t) dt; x(t) = Σ c_n e^(j2πnf₀t).

cards.f: Fourier series of an even signal
cards.b: Contains only the constant and cosine terms (b_n = 0).
x(t + T/2) = −x(t): the series contains only odd harmonics.
(4A/π)[sin ω₀t + (1/3) sin 3ω₀t + (1/5) sin 5ω₀t + …]: odd harmonics with amplitude 4A/(nπ).
Average power = Σ|c_n|² = a₀² + Σ(a_n² + b_n²)/2.
A truncated Fourier series overshoots near a jump by about 9 % of the jump, regardless of the number of terms.

cards.f: Line spacing in the spectrum of a periodic signal
cards.b: Equal to the fundamental frequency f₀ = 1/T.
X(f) = ∫x(t)e^(−j2πft)dt; inverse x(t) = ∫X(f)e^(j2πft)df.

cards.f: Transform of a rectangular pulse (height 1, width τ)
cards.b: τ sinc(fτ), with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx); first nulls at f = ±1/τ.
x(t − t₀) ↔ X(f)e^(−j2πft₀): magnitude unchanged, linear phase added.
x(t)cos(2πf_ct) ↔ ½[X(f − f_c) + X(f + f_c)].
x(at) ↔ (1/|a|)X(f/a): compressing in time expands in frequency.
x(t) * y(t) ↔ X(f)Y(f); multiplication in time ↔ convolution in frequency.
1 for all f: an impulse contains all frequencies equally.

cards.f: Spectrum symmetry of a real signal
cards.b: X(−f) = X*(f): even magnitude, odd phase.
y(t) = ∫x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ: the output of an LTI system with impulse response h(t).
Y(f) = H(f)X(f), where H(f) is the Fourier transform of h(t).

cards.f: Causality condition for an LTI system
cards.b: h(t) = 0 for t < 0.

cards.f: BIBO stability condition for an LTI system
cards.b: ∫|h(t)|dt is finite.

cards.f: Response of an LTI system to A cos(2πft)
cards.b: A|H(f)| cos(2πft + ∠H(f)): same frequency, scaled and phase-shifted.
H(f) = Ke^(−j2πft_d) over the signal band: constant gain and linear phase, giving output Kx(t − t_d).
cos A cos B = ½[cos(A − B) + cos(A + B)].

cards.f: Can an LTI system create new frequencies?
cards.b: No; only non-linear or time-varying systems (e.g. mixers, distorting amplifiers) can.
I = log₂(1/p) bits for an event of probability p.
H = −Σp_i log₂ p_i bits/symbol; maximum log₂ M for M equiprobable symbols.
C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bits/s for an AWGN channel of bandwidth B; S/N as a linear power ratio.
The average code length per symbol of a lossless code cannot be less than the source entropy H, but can approach it.
At most 2B symbols/s through an ideal baseband channel of bandwidth B without ISI; bit rate ≤ 2B log₂ M.
No codeword is the beginning of another, so a bit stream can be decoded unambiguously without separators.

cards.f: Entropy of a binary source with p = 0.1
AM modulation index from the envelope
cards.b: μ = (A_max − A_min)/(A_max + A_min); μ ≤ 1 for distortion-free envelope detection.
Total power P_c(1 + μ²/2); efficiency μ²/(2 + μ²), at most 1/3 at μ = 1.

cards.f: Bandwidths of AM, DSB-SC and SSB
cards.b: AM and DSB-SC: 2W. SSB: W (W = message bandwidth).

cards.f: Coherent detection of DSB-SC with phase error φ
cards.b: Output ∝ m(t)cos φ; at φ = 90° the output vanishes.
s(t) = m(t)cos ω_ct ∓ m̂(t)sin ω_ct; minus gives the upper sideband, plus the lower.
FM bandwidth B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) = 2(β + 1)f_m.
f_image = f_LO + f_IF = f_RF + 2f_IF; it must be filtered out before the mixer.
Choose 1/f_c ≪ RC ≪ 1/W so the output follows the envelope but not the carrier.
A signal band-limited to W Hz is recoverable from samples taken at f_s > 2W.
Components above f_s/2 fold to |f − kf_s|; e.g. 7 kHz sampled at 10 kHz appears at 3 kHz. Prevented by an anti-aliasing filter.
n f_s for n bits per sample; telephony 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kb/s.

cards.f: SQNR of a uniform n-bit quantiser (full-scale sine)
cards.b: ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB: about 6 dB per bit.

cards.f: Bits per symbol of M-ary modulation
cards.b: log₂ M; R_b = R_s log₂ M.
Adjacent constellation points differ in only one bit, so the most likely symbol error causes one bit error.
B = R_s(1 + α), with roll-off factor 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.
s(t) = I(t)cos(2πf_ct) − Q(t)sin(2πf_ct); recover I with 2cos and LPF, Q with −2sin and LPF.
N = kTB; at 290 K about −174 dBm/Hz, so about −114 dBm in 1 MHz.
L_fs = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) dB (far field, isotropic antennas); rises 6 dB per doubling of distance or frequency.
P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r − L_fs − other losses (all in dB units).
F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + … (linear values): first stage dominates.
E_b/N₀ = SNR × B/R_b.

cards.f: BER of coherent BPSK in AWGN
cards.b: P_b = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)); about 10⁻⁵ at E_b/N₀ ≈ 9.6 dB.

cards.f: Why put a low-noise amplifier first?
cards.b: By the Friis formula the first stage's noise figure adds directly while later stages' contributions are divided by the preceding gain.

questions.q: An amplifier has a voltage gain of 100 (input and output across the same impedance). What is its gain in dB?
questions.why: For an amplitude ratio, gain = 20 log₁₀(100) = 40 dB (power gain 10⁴). 20 dB uses 10 log₁₀, the power formula, on a voltage ratio. 100 dB quotes the linear gain as if it were already in dB. 10 dB is the value for a power ratio of 10, not a voltage ratio of 100.

questions.q: A transmitter output of 2 W is expressed in dBm. Which is correct?
questions.why: 2 W = 2000 mW, and 10 log₁₀(2000) ≈ 33 dBm (30 dBm for 1 W plus 3 dB for doubling). 3 dBm is the value in dBW mislabelled as dBm. 63 dBm adds 60 dB, as if converting from microwatts. 36 dBm uses 20 log₁₀ for the doubling (an amplitude formula) on a power ratio.

questions.q: A signal x(t) = 4 cos(2π × 1000t) + 2 cos(2π × 3000t) V is applied to a 1 Ω reference. Sketch its two-sided amplitude spectrum and find its average power and rms value.
markScheme: Spectral lines of height 2 at ±1 kHz and height 1 at ±3 kHz
Power of each component A²/2: 8 W and 2 W
Components at different frequencies: powers add, total 10 W
questions.modelAnswer: The two-sided spectrum has lines of amplitude 2 at ±1 kHz and amplitude 1 at ±3 kHz (half of each cosine amplitude at each sign of frequency). Because the components have different frequencies their cross-term averages to zero, so powers add: 4²/2 + 2²/2 = 8 + 2 = 10 W (normalised to 1 Ω). The rms value is √10 ≈ 3.16 V.

questions.q: A ±1 V square wave (odd, 50 % duty) has fundamental frequency 1 kHz. What is the amplitude of its 3 kHz component?
questions.why: b_n = 4A/(nπ), so for n = 3 the amplitude is 4/(3π) ≈ 0.42 V. 0.33 V is simply 1/3, missing the 4/π factor. 1.27 V is 4/π, the fundamental amplitude. 0 V would be correct for even harmonics, but the third harmonic is odd and present.

questions.q: What fraction of the average power of a ±1 square wave lies in its fundamental component?
questions.why: Total power is 1; the fundamental has amplitude 4/π, so its power is (4/π)²/2 ≈ 0.81. About 64 % is 2/π ≈ 0.637 (or 4/π divided by 2), using the amplitude instead of the power. About 100 % ignores the harmonics. About 50 % uses amplitude²/2 with an amplitude of 1, i.e. treating the fundamental as having the square wave's height.

questions.q: Find the trigonometric Fourier series of the odd square wave x(t) = +A for 0 < t < T/2 and −A for T/2 < t < T, and use Parseval's theorem to find the fraction of power in harmonics up to and including the fifth.
markScheme: Odd function: a₀ = 0 and a_n = 0
b_n = (2/T)[∫₀^(T/2) A sin(nω₀t)dt − ∫_(T/2)^T A sin(nω₀t)dt] = (2A/nπ)(1 − cos nπ)
b_n = 4A/(nπ) for odd n, 0 for even n
Total power A²; harmonic powers (b_n)²/2
questions.modelAnswer: The wave is odd, so a₀ = a_n = 0. With ω₀ = 2π/T, b_n = (2/T)[∫₀^(T/2) A sin nω₀t dt − ∫_(T/2)^T A sin nω₀t dt] = (2A/(nπ))(1 − cos nπ). This is 4A/(nπ) for odd n and 0 for even n. The total power is A² (the signal is ±A always). The power in harmonic n is b_n²/2 = 8A²/(n²π²). Summing n = 1, 3, 5: (8/π²)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25)A² ≈ 0.811 × 1.151 A² ≈ 0.933A², so about 93 % of the power lies in the first three non-zero harmonics.

questions.q: A rectangular pulse lasts 0.5 ms. Where are the first nulls of its spectrum?
questions.why: The transform τ sinc(fτ) first falls to zero at f = ±1/τ = ±1/(0.5 × 10⁻³) = ±2 kHz. ±318 Hz divides 1/τ by 2π, as if 1/τ were an angular frequency in rad/s. ±1 kHz is 1/(2τ), halving the correct value as if the null-to-null width were 1/τ. ±4 kHz is the full null-to-null main-lobe width 2/τ, not the position of the first null.

questions.q: If x(t) has Fourier transform X(f), what is the transform of x(t − 2 ms)?
questions.why: A delay of t₀ multiplies the spectrum by e^(−j2πft₀), here with t₀ = 0.002 s: magnitude unchanged, phase falling linearly with frequency. X(f − 500 Hz) is a frequency shift, which needs multiplication by e^(j2π500t) in time, not a delay. The positive exponent corresponds to an advance of 2 ms, not a delay. Dividing by 2 confuses delay with time scaling.

questions.q: Using transform properties (not direct integration), find and sketch the spectrum of y(t) = p(t)cos(2πf_ct), where p(t) is a rectangular pulse of unit height and width τ = 1 ms centred on t = 0, and f_c = 100 kHz. State the bandwidth of the main lobe.
markScheme: P(f) = τ sinc(fτ) = 10⁻³ sinc(10⁻³ f)
Modulation property: Y(f) = ½[P(f − f_c) + P(f + f_c)]
Sketch: sinc shapes centred at ±100 kHz, peak 0.5 × 10⁻³, nulls at ±1 kHz from centre
Main lobe 99–101 kHz: bandwidth 2/τ = 2 kHz
questions.modelAnswer: The pulse has P(f) = τ sinc(fτ) = 10⁻³ sinc(10⁻³f). By the modulation property, multiplying by cos(2πf_ct) gives Y(f) = ½[P(f − f_c) + P(f + f_c)] = 0.5 × 10⁻³[sinc(10⁻³(f − 10⁵)) + sinc(10⁻³(f + 10⁵))]. The sketch shows two sinc shapes, peak 0.5 × 10⁻³ V/Hz, centred on ±100 kHz, each with first nulls 1 kHz either side of centre. The main lobe runs from 99 to 101 kHz, a null-to-null bandwidth of 2/τ = 2 kHz, twice the baseband first-null frequency.

questions.q: The discrete-time sequence x = [1, 2, 1] is applied to an LTI system with impulse response h = [1, 1]. What is the output?
questions.why: y[n] = Σx[k]h[n − k]: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 2 + 1 = 3, y[2] = 1 + 2 = 3, y[3] = 1, so [1, 3, 3, 1]. [1, 2, 1, 0] treats h as a single impulse, ignoring its second tap. [1, 2, 1] is element-wise multiplication of x by h padded with ones, not convolution. [1, 3, 3] truncates the output to the input length, dropping the final term; full convolution has length 3 + 2 − 1 = 4.

questions.q: A sinusoid at twice the cut-off frequency passes through a first-order RC low-pass filter, H(f) = 1/(1 + j2πfRC). What are the gain and phase shift?
questions.why: At f = 2f_c, 2πfRC = 2, so H = 1/(1 + j2): |H| = 1/√5 ≈ 0.447 and ∠H = −arctan 2 ≈ −63.4°. 0.707 and −45° are the values at the cut-off itself. 0.5 and −90° treat the filter as falling exactly in proportion to 1/f with a full −90° shift, which only holds asymptotically at f ≫ f_c. 0.447 and +63.4° has the right gain but the phase sign of a high-pass (lead) network.

questions.q: State the conditions for distortionless transmission through an LTI channel, and explain why a channel with non-linear phase causes problems for a digital data link even if its gain is flat.
markScheme: Over the signal band: |H(f)| = K (constant)
Phase ∠H(f) = −2πft_d, linear in f (constant delay t_d)
Output then y(t) = Kx(t − t_d)
Non-linear phase → different frequency components delayed by different amounts (group delay varies)
Pulses spread out in time → intersymbol interference → bit errors; equalisation may be needed
questions.modelAnswer: An LTI channel is distortionless over a signal's band if H(f) = Ke^(−j2πft_d) there: constant magnitude K and phase falling linearly with frequency, which corresponds to a pure delay t_d, so y(t) = Kx(t − t_d). If the phase is not linear, different frequency components are delayed by different amounts even when the gain is flat. A rectangular data pulse is made of many components, so it emerges smeared out in time. The tails of each pulse overlap neighbouring symbols, causing intersymbol interference and raising the bit error rate; an equaliser is then needed to correct the phase response.

questions.q: A source emits four symbols with probabilities ½, ¼, ⅛ and ⅛. What is its entropy?
questions.why: H = ½·1 + ¼·2 + ⅛·3 + ⅛·3 = 1.75 bits/symbol. 2 bits is log₂ 4, the maximum, which applies only if all four symbols are equally likely. 1 bit is the information in the most likely symbol alone. 1.5 bits counts the two ⅛ symbols as carrying 2 bits each instead of 3.

questions.q: A channel has bandwidth 1 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB. What is its Shannon capacity?
questions.why: 20 dB is a power ratio of 100, so C = 10⁶ × log₂(101) ≈ 6.66 Mb/s. About 20 Mb/s puts the dB value straight into the formula as if C = B × SNR(dB). About 4.4 Mb/s uses log₂(1 + 20), treating 20 dB as a linear ratio of 20. About 4.6 Mb/s uses the natural logarithm (ln 101 ≈ 4.62) instead of log₂, which does not give bits.

questions.q: For a source with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125: (a) compute its entropy; (b) design a Huffman code and find its average length; (c) compare with a fixed-length code and comment.
markScheme: Huffman: merge the two 0.125s → 0.25, merge with 0.25 → 0.5, merge with 0.5
Codewords e.g. 0, 10, 110, 111
Average length = 1.75 bits/symbol = H (probabilities are powers of ½)
Fixed-length needs 2 bits; Huffman saves 12.5 %; code is prefix-free
questions.modelAnswer: (a) H = 0.5 log₂2 + 0.25 log₂4 + 2 × 0.125 log₂8 = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.75 = 1.75 bits/symbol. (b) Huffman: combine the two least likely symbols (0.125 + 0.125 = 0.25), then combine with the 0.25 symbol (0.5), then with the 0.5 symbol. Assigning 0/1 at each split gives codewords 0, 10, 110, 111. Average length = 0.5 × 1 + 0.25 × 2 + 0.125 × 3 + 0.125 × 3 = 1.75 bits. (c) A fixed-length code needs 2 bits per symbol, so Huffman saves 12.5 % and here reaches the entropy limit exactly because all probabilities are powers of ½. The code is prefix-free, so it decodes without separators.

questions.q: An AM signal's envelope varies between a maximum of 15 V and a minimum of 5 V. What is the modulation index?
questions.why: μ = (A_max − A_min)/(A_max + A_min) = (15 − 5)/(15 + 5) = 0.5. 0.33 is A_min/A_max. 0.67 is (15 − 5)/15, dividing by the maximum instead of the sum. 2 inverts the ratio, which would also imply overmodulation.

questions.q: What fraction of the total transmitted power of a tone-modulated AM signal with μ = 0.5 is in the sidebands?
questions.why: Efficiency = μ²/(2 + μ²) = 0.25/2.25 ≈ 11 %. About 25 % is μ² alone, forgetting both the ½ per-sideband factor and the carrier power in the denominator. About 33 % is the maximum efficiency, for μ = 1. About 50 % assumes the carrier and sidebands share the power equally.

questions.q: Show that a phasing SSB modulator with inputs cos(2πf_mt) and sin(2πf_mt) and carriers cos(2πf_ct) and sin(2πf_ct) produces only the upper sideband when the two products are subtracted. Sketch the block diagram and state the main practical difficulty.
markScheme: Block diagram: message → mixer with cos ω_ct; message shifted −90° → mixer with sin ω_ct (carrier via 90° shifter); subtractor
cos ω_mt cos ω_ct = ½[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t + cos(ω_c + ω_m)t]
sin ω_mt sin ω_ct = ½[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t − cos(ω_c + ω_m)t]
Difference = cos(ω_c + ω_m)t: lower sideband cancels, upper remains (sum gives LSB)
Difficulty: needs accurate 90° shift over the whole message band (Hilbert transformer) and balanced gains, otherwise imperfect sideband suppression
questions.modelAnswer: The block diagram has two branches: the message multiplied by cos ω_ct, and the message passed through a −90° (Hilbert) shifter multiplied by sin ω_ct (the carrier delayed by 90°), followed by a subtractor. For a tone, the upper branch gives cos ω_mt cos ω_ct = ½[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t + cos(ω_c + ω_m)t]; the lower gives sin ω_mt sin ω_ct = ½[cos(ω_c − ω_m)t − cos(ω_c + ω_m)t]. Subtracting cancels the difference-frequency (lower sideband) terms and leaves cos(ω_c + ω_m)t, the upper sideband; adding would keep the lower sideband. The practical difficulty is producing an accurate 90° shift for every frequency in the message band, with matched gains in both branches; any error leaves a residual unwanted sideband.

questions.q: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz without an anti-aliasing filter. At what frequency does it appear after reconstruction?
questions.why: Since 7 kHz exceeds f_s/2 = 5 kHz, it aliases to |7 − 10| = 3 kHz. 7 kHz would be correct only if f_s exceeded 14 kHz. 17 kHz is the sum f + f_s, a spectral image that the reconstruction filter removes. 5 kHz is the folding frequency f_s/2 itself, not where the tone lands.

questions.q: A 16-QAM system runs at 1 Mbaud with raised-cosine filtering, roll-off α = 0.25. What are its bit rate and passband bandwidth?
questions.why: 16-QAM carries log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol, so R_b = 4 Mb/s, and B = R_s(1 + α) = 1.25 MHz. 16 Mb/s multiplies the symbol rate by M instead of log₂ M. 0.625 MHz uses the baseband bandwidth R_s(1 + α)/2, which applies before up-conversion, not to the passband signal. 1 Mb/s confuses the symbol rate with the bit rate.

questions.q: Draw and explain a block diagram of a 16-QAM modulator and the matching coherent demodulator, using s(t) = I(t)cos(2πf_ct) − Q(t)sin(2πf_ct). Show mathematically how the demodulator recovers I(t).
markScheme: Modulator: serial-to-parallel (2 bits → I, 2 bits → Q), Gray-coded 4-level mappers (±1, ±3), pulse-shaping filters
Modulator: I × cos ω_ct, Q × (carrier shifted 90°, sin ω_ct), subtract to form s(t)
Demodulator: split, multiply by 2cos ω_ct and −2sin ω_ct from phase-locked LO, low-pass filter, sample, decide nearest point
s(t)·2cos ω_ct = I(1 + cos 2ω_ct) − Q sin 2ω_ct
Low-pass filter removes 2ω_c terms leaving I(t)
Need carrier phase and symbol timing recovery
questions.modelAnswer: Modulator: the bit stream is split by a serial-to-parallel converter into pairs for the I branch and pairs for the Q branch. Each pair is Gray-mapped to one of four levels (−3, −1, +1, +3) and pulse-shaped. The I signal multiplies cos ω_ct; the Q signal multiplies sin ω_ct, obtained from the same oscillator via a 90° shifter, and is subtracted, giving s(t) = I cos ω_ct − Q sin ω_ct. Demodulator: the received signal is split and multiplied by 2cos ω_ct and by −2sin ω_ct from a local oscillator phase-locked to the carrier, each product is low-pass filtered, then sampled at the symbol centres and the nearest constellation point chosen. Recovering I: s(t) × 2cos ω_ct = 2I cos² ω_ct − 2Q sin ω_ct cos ω_ct = I(1 + cos 2ω_ct) − Q sin 2ω_ct. The low-pass filter removes the 2ω_c terms, leaving I(t). Similarly the −2sin branch leaves Q(t). Carrier phase and symbol timing must be recovered or the constellation rotates and smears.

questions.q: What is the thermal noise power in a 1 MHz bandwidth at 290 K?
questions.why: kT at 290 K is −174 dBm/Hz, and 10 log₁₀(10⁶) = 60 dB, so N ≈ −174 + 60 = −114 dBm. About −174 dBm is the density per hertz, not the power in 1 MHz. About −144 dBm is −174 + 30, i.e. adding 30 dB as if 1 MHz were 10³ Hz. About −84 dBm adds 90 dB, treating the bandwidth as 1 GHz.

questions.q: A link has SNR = 16 dB in a bandwidth of 36 MHz and carries 57.6 Mb/s. What is E_b/N₀ in dB?
questions.why: E_b/N₀ = SNR × B/R_b; in dB, 16 + 10 log₁₀(36/57.6) = 16 − 2.0 ≈ 14 dB. About 16 dB assumes E_b/N₀ equals the SNR, ignoring the rate-to-bandwidth ratio. About 18 dB applies the ratio the wrong way round (R_b/B). About 12 dB uses 20 log₁₀(57.6/36) ≈ 4.1 dB for the rate correction, an amplitude-style formula applied to a power ratio.

questions.q: A geostationary satellite downlink at 12 GHz has a path length of 36 000 km, transmit power 100 W, transmit antenna gain 30 dBi, receive antenna gain 40 dBi, system noise temperature 150 K and bandwidth 36 MHz. Calculate the free-space path loss, the received power, the noise power and the SNR.
markScheme: States free-space, far-field assumption and no other losses
questions.modelAnswer: λ = 3 × 10⁸/12 × 10⁹ = 0.025 m. L_fs = 20 log₁₀(4π × 3.6 × 10⁷/0.025) = 20 log₁₀(1.81 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 205.2 dB. With P_t = 100 W = 20 dBW, P_r = 20 + 30 + 40 − 205.2 ≈ −115.2 dBW (about 3.0 × 10⁻¹² W). The noise power is N = kTB = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ × 150 × 36 × 10⁶ ≈ 7.46 × 10⁻¹⁴ W ≈ −131.3 dBW. So SNR ≈ −115.2 + 131.3 ≈ 16.1 dB. This assumes free-space propagation in the far field with no atmospheric, rain or pointing losses, which in practice would add a few dB of margin requirement.

questions.q:
A 1 MHz carrier is amplitude modulated by a 5 kHz tone. On an oscilloscope the envelope varies between 15 V and 5 V; the signal is developed across 50 Ω.
(a) Find the modulation index and the carrier amplitude, and write an expression for s(t). [4]
(b) Sketch the one-sided amplitude spectrum, labelling frequencies and amplitudes, and state the bandwidth. [4]
(c) Find the carrier power, total power and power efficiency. [4]
(d) The same tone is instead sent as SSB using a phasing modulator. Derive which sideband is produced by s(t) = cos(2πf_mt)cos(2πf_ct) − sin(2πf_mt)sin(2πf_ct), and state its bandwidth advantage. [4]
(e) In a superheterodyne receiver tuned to this 1 MHz signal with an IF of 455 kHz and the LO above the signal, find the LO frequency and the image frequency. [4]
markScheme: (b) Lines: 10 V at 1000 kHz; 2.5 V at 995 kHz and 1005 kHz; bandwidth 10 kHz
(d) Identity cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B gives cos(2π(f_c + f_m)t): upper sideband only at 1.005 MHz
(d) Bandwidth W = 5 kHz, half that of AM; no carrier power wasted
(e) Image = f_LO + IF = 1910 kHz; must be rejected by RF filtering before the mixer
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For tone AM the envelope is A_c(1 ± μ). So A_c(1 + μ) = 15 and A_c(1 − μ) = 5, giving A_c = 10 V and μ = 0.5 (equivalently μ = (15 − 5)/(15 + 5)). Hence s(t) = 10[1 + 0.5 cos(2π × 5000t)] cos(2π × 10⁶t) V.

(b) Expanding: s(t) = 10 cos(2π × 10⁶t) + 2.5 cos(2π × 1.005 × 10⁶t) + 2.5 cos(2π × 0.995 × 10⁶t). The one-sided spectrum has a 10 V line at 1000 kHz and 2.5 V lines (μA_c/2) at 995 kHz and 1005 kHz. Bandwidth = 2f_m = 10 kHz.

(c) Carrier power P_c = A_c²/(2R) = 100/(2 × 50) = 1 W. Each sideband has amplitude 2.5 V, power 6.25/100 = 0.0625 W, so the sidebands total 0.125 W (= μ²P_c/2). Total power = 1.125 W. Efficiency = 0.125/1.125 ≈ 11.1 % (= μ²/(2 + μ²)); nearly 89 % of the power is in the information-free carrier.

(d) Using cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B with A = 2πf_ct and B = 2πf_mt, s(t) = cos(2π(f_c + f_m)t): a single line at 1.005 MHz, the upper sideband. The lower-sideband terms ½cos(2π(f_c − f_m)t) from the two products cancel. SSB needs only W = 5 kHz of bandwidth, half that of AM, and spends no power on the carrier, though it requires coherent detection.

(e) With the LO above the signal, f_LO = f_RF + f_IF = 1000 + 455 = 1455 kHz. The image is the other frequency that mixes to 455 kHz: f_LO + f_IF = 1910 kHz (= f_RF + 2f_IF). A station there would be received on top of the wanted one unless the RF front-end filter attenuates it before the mixer.

questions.q:
A satellite transponder offers 36 MHz of bandwidth with an SNR of 16.1 dB at the receiver (AWGN).
(a) Calculate the Shannon capacity of the channel. [4]
(b) A designer uses raised-cosine pulses with α = 0.25. Find the maximum symbol rate, and the bit rate for QPSK and for 16-QAM. Compare both with the capacity. [5]
(c) Sketch a block diagram of the QPSK/16-QAM modulator, explaining the role of each block. [5]
(d) For QPSK, find E_b/N₀ and estimate the bit error rate using P_b = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)). Explain qualitatively why 16-QAM at its higher bit rate would have a much higher BER. [6]
markScheme: (b) QPSK: 57.6 Mb/s; 16-QAM: 115.2 Mb/s; both below 194 Mb/s, so permitted by Shannon
(c) Serial-to-parallel, Gray mapping to I/Q levels, pulse-shaping filters, mixers with cos and 90°-shifted carrier, subtractor/summer, (RF amplifier)
(d) 16-QAM: twice the bit rate halves E_b/N₀ (≈ 11.0 dB) and constellation points are closer for the same average power, so the error probability rises sharply
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) SNR = 10^(16.1/10) ≈ 40.7. C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 36 × 10⁶ × log₂(41.7) ≈ 36 × 10⁶ × 5.38 ≈ 194 Mb/s. This is the maximum error-free rate achievable with ideal coding.

(b) With raised-cosine pulses the passband bandwidth is R_s(1 + α), so R_s = 36/1.25 = 28.8 Mbaud. QPSK carries 2 bits/symbol: 57.6 Mb/s. 16-QAM carries 4 bits/symbol: 115.2 Mb/s. Both are below the 194 Mb/s capacity, so Shannon's theorem does not rule them out; their spectral efficiencies are 1.6 and 3.2 b/s/Hz against a limit of about 5.4 b/s/Hz.

(c) The bit stream enters a serial-to-parallel converter, which sends alternate bits (QPSK) or bit pairs (16-QAM) to the I and Q branches. Gray-coded mappers convert them to amplitude levels (±1 for QPSK; ±1, ±3 for 16-QAM). Raised-cosine pulse-shaping filters limit the bandwidth and control intersymbol interference. The I branch multiplies cos ω_ct from the local oscillator; the Q branch multiplies the oscillator output shifted by 90° (sin ω_ct). The branches are combined (s = I cos ω_ct − Q sin ω_ct) and passed to the up-converter and power amplifier.

(d) For QPSK, E_b/N₀ = SNR × B/R_b = 40.7 × 36/57.6 ≈ 25.5, about 14.1 dB. With Gray coding and coherent detection in AWGN, P_b = Q(√(2 × 25.5)) = Q(7.14) ≈ 5 × 10⁻¹³, effectively error-free. For 16-QAM, doubling the bit rate halves E_b/N₀ to about 12.7 (11.0 dB). In addition, packing 16 points into the same average power puts neighbouring points much closer together than the four QPSK points, so a smaller noise excursion causes a symbol error. Both effects push 16-QAM far up its BER curve; it would typically need several dB more E_b/N₀ than QPSK for the same BER, so the designer trades throughput against error rate, or adds error-correcting coding.
